name: Question 15
problem: Let $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-y.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,-1).$
worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,-1)+∇f(0,-1)\cdot ⟨x,y+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(0,-1)=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =4x\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(0,-1)=0, \\ {f}_{y} & =-1 &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(0,-1)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(0,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(0,-1) & =⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,-1)+∇f(0,-1)\cdot ⟨x,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x,y+1⟩ \\  & ≈1+0-(y+1) \\  & ≈-y.\end{aligned}
$$

html:
Question 15
?

Let f(x,y)=2x2−y. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (0,−1).

a
f(x,y)≈2x−y
b
f(x,y)≈−y
c
f(x,y)≈1−2x
d
f(x,y)≈−1+2x−2y
e
f(x,y)≈3+x+2y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b) is given by f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅⟨x−a,y−b⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (0,−1) is f(x,y)≈f(0,−1)+∇f(0,−1)⋅⟨x,y+1⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(0,−1)=1. Computing the partial derivatives, we get fx=4x⇒fx(0,−1)=0,fy=−1⇒fy(0,−1)=−1.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (0,−1) is given by ∇f(0,−1)=⟨0,−1⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is f(x,y)≈f(0,−1)+∇f(0,−1)⋅⟨x,y+1⟩≈1+⟨0,−1⟩⋅⟨x,y+1⟩≈1+0−(y+1)≈−y.
